newsitem.title: USA: DeBakey says Yeltsin surgery may be next week.
newsitem.headline: DeBakey says Yeltsin surgery may be next week.

text.p: Eminent U.S. heart surgeon Michael DeBakey said on Tuesday that surgery on Russian President Boris Yeltsin's heart might be performed next week, although no date had been set.
He told Reuters he would go to Russia later this week to examine Yeltsin and meet his medical team to make sure his health was strong enough for the operation.
"We're shooting for next week," said DeBakey, who will act as a consultant during the surgery.

Yeltsin, 65, is recuperating from earlier heart attacks and is scheduled to have bypass surgery to improve blood flow to his heart. DeBakey, 88, who pioneered the heart bypass procedure, examined Yeltsin last month in Russia and predicted a full recovery for the stricken leader, but recommended putting off the operation until he was stronger.
Asked if Yeltsin's health was now good enough for the surgery, DeBakey said, "I hope so. I can't say definitely until I get there. That's one of the reasons I'm going to check on all that."
He told CNN that, following his visit in late September, Yeltsin's medical team set a six-week window for the surgery, contingent on improvements in his health.
"It's now believed that most of the things (health problems) are corrected, that his condition has improved and probably he will be ready this coming week," DeBakey said.
"It's not that we're doing it any earlier than we planned, it's just simply within that period that we planned," he said.
DeBakey said that Yeltsin would need a multiple bypass operation because of clogging in the arteries to his heart.
The surgery will be performed by Russian cardiologist Renat Akchurin, who trained under DeBakey. DeBakey maintains a full schedule of surgery and teaches at the Baylor College of Medicine in Houston.
At DeBakey's request, Akchurin visited Houston recently to familiarize himself with support equipment to be used during the operation. DeBakey said the equipment has now been sent to Moscow.
In Russia, the Kremlin began on Tuesday issuing what it said would be regular medical bulletins about Yeltsin's condition.

"From this week the final stage of the preparation for President Boris Yeltsin's operation has begun. Various degrees of functional tests will be undertaken and there will be round-the-clock monitoring," the bulletin said.
"The main aim of the final stage of the preparation is to bring the patient to the peak of his current physical and physiological capabilities," it said.
